src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:30 — [confidence 100][P1] `for i = 0, 1000 do` truncates redirect traversal even though evicting payloads does not remove redirect nodes, so a trace chain deeper than 1,001 spans is split at an arbitrary ancestor and flushed as disconnected segments.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the loop limit was reduced from 10000 to 1000 (line 30), while the span count limit enforced via zpopmin is also 1000 (lines 55-57). The redirect hash (main_redirect_key) stores parent-child relationships that are not cleaned up when spans are evicted via zpopmin. This means if a trace has more than 1000 spans in a chain, the redirect traversal will hit the 1000 iteration limit before finding the root, causing spans to be grouped incorrectly. The original comment even noted 'theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly' - reducing this to 1000 while also limiting spans to 1000 creates a real consistency issue where deep traces will be split.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:62 — [confidence 100][P2] `if span_count > 1000 then` duplicates the segment-size policy outside `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans`, so configured limits are ignored during insertion and the next limit change requires synchronized edits in Python and Lua to avoid silently retaining the wrong number of spans.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the Lua script now has a hardcoded limit of 1000 spans (line 62: `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000)`), while the Python code in buffer.py has a configurable `max_segment_spans` parameter. The diff shows the Python code previously had span count checking (lines 446-452 were removed) that used `self.max_segment_spans`. Now the Lua script enforces a hardcoded 1000 limit during insertion, creating a synchronization issue where changing the Python config won't affect the Lua behavior. This is a legitimate architectural concern about configuration duplication, not a bug per se since the code will function, but it's a real maintainability issue grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:47 — [confidence 75][P2] `redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` uses Redis's default `AGGREGATE SUM`, so a retried payload present in both sets receives the sum of two epoch timestamps and is ordered as newer than all legitimate spans, causing eviction to discard a different span and retain stale duplicate data.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows zunionstore being used at lines 47 and 52 in add-buffer.lua without specifying AGGREGATE option, which defaults to SUM. The code uses end_timestamp_precise as scores (seen in buffer.py line 196: `p.zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise for span in subsegment})`). If the same span payload exists in both sets being unioned (e.g., due to retry), their timestamps would be summed, creating an artificially high score. Combined with the zpopmin eviction at line 61 that removes spans with lowest scores when count > 1000, this could cause incorrect ordering and eviction behavior. The finding correctly identifies a real bug in the Redis aggregation logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:61 — [P1, confidence 100] The hard-coded `if span_count > 1000 then` bypasses the public `max_segment_spans` setting in `SpansBuffer.__init__`, so deployments configured below 1,000 flush segments larger than their stated safety limit and the removed flush-time check no longer rejects them.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in add-buffer.lua, a hard-coded limit of 1000 is used (line 61: 'if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin'). Meanwhile, in buffer.py, the code that previously checked 'if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans' has been removed (lines 446-452 in the old code are gone). The SpansBuffer class has a configurable max_segment_spans parameter (visible in the context), but the Lua script uses a hard-coded 1000. This means if max_segment_spans is configured to be less than 1000, the Lua script will allow more spans than the configured limit, and the Python-side check that would have caught this is now removed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:197 — [P1, confidence 100] `p.zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise for span in subsegment})` writes sorted-set commands to the existing `span-buf:s:*` namespace without a key-version migration or dual-read/write window, so every still-live set created by the previous release raises Redis `WRONGTYPE` during rolling deployment and aborts ingestion or flushing until that buffered data expires.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a clear change from Redis SET commands (sadd, scard, sscan, sunionstore) to SORTED SET commands (zadd, zcard, zscan, zunionstore) on the same key namespace 'span-buf:s:*'. In buffer.py line 197, the code changes from p.sadd() to p.zadd(). In the Lua script add-buffer.lua, commands change from scard/sunionstore to zcard/zunionstore. During a rolling deployment, old code may have created keys as SETs, and new code will try to operate on them as SORTED SETs, causing Redis WRONGTYPE errors. There's no migration strategy or key versioning visible in the diff to handle this transition.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is correct. In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key() at line 840, the code does `value = getattr(item, self.key)` where self.key is 'datetime' (from order_by='-datetime' in the endpoint). It then calls `math.floor(value)` or `math.ceil(value)` on a datetime object, which will raise TypeError since math.floor/ceil don't accept datetime objects. The DateTimePaginator handles this correctly by converting to timestamp, but OptimizedCursorPaginator doesn't. This would cause 500 errors for any admin using optimized_pagination=true on the audit logs endpoint.
